title: The shipwreck (Acts 27–28)
hookLine: two weeks of storm, Paul breaks bread on deck, 276 swim to Malta, and a viper bites harmlessly

lines: A PRISONER ON A CARGO SHIP.
cards: Some weeks are all storm, and you can't see the sky. Now board a cargo ship in the Mediterranean, late in the sailing season.
Paul is aboard as a prisoner, not a passenger, taken to Rome for trial under a Roman officer named Julius. Paul warns it's too late in the year to sail. Nobody listens.

Then a violent wind sweeps off Crete; the ship is caught and can't turn into it. They lash ropes around the hull to hold it together, throw the cargo overboard, then the ship's gear. Day after day, no sun, no stars.
Luke, writing as we, as if aboard, says all hope that we should be saved was taken away.

teach.b: Paul stands among the exhausted crew: in the King James Bible, "And now I exhort you to be of good cheer: for there shall be no loss of any man's life among you, but of the ship." An angel stood by me last night, he says.
Again: "Wherefore, sirs, be of good cheer: for I believe God." Be of good cheer is the King James wording; the Greek means something like be good-spirited. Take heart.
On the fourteenth night they sense land. Some sailors try to slip away in the lifeboat, and are stopped. Before dawn, everyone starving and terrified, Paul does something ordinary: tells them to eat.
Two weeks without a real meal, he says; this is for your health.

teach.h: HE TOOK BREAD, AND GAVE THANKS.
teach.b: Then "he took bread, and gave thanks to God in presence of them all: and when he had broken it, he began to eat."
Took, gave thanks, broke: Luke's words for anamnesis, now on a storm-battered deck, among soldiers, sailors and prisoners.
All take heart and eat; Luke counts two hundred and seventy-six people. At daybreak the ship runs aground and breaks apart. Swimmers jump first; the rest float in on planks.
It's Malta; the islanders build a fire in the cold rain. A viper comes out of the firewood and fastens onto Paul's hand. The locals decide he must be a murderer.
He shakes it into the fire, nothing happens, and they change their minds: he must be a god.

how: Many Christians give thanks before meals, as Paul does on the deck. In Malta, Paul's shipwreck is remembered every February 10 with a public holiday and feast, and Maltese tradition traces the island's faith to it.

games.q: you're Paul. fourteen days of storm, nobody's eaten, and dawn is coming. what do you tell the ship?
o: fast and pray until the storm ends.
eat something. this is for your health.
games.why: he urges them all to eat, takes bread, gives thanks in front of everyone, breaks it and begins to eat. then they all take heart.

practice: If you have something near, bread, a cracker, fruit, a cup of tea, hold it before you eat; if not, picture it. If you pray, give thanks for it, as Paul did; if not, notice where it came from, and how many hands it passed through.
Then eat slowly, like someone who hasn't eaten in a while, and let it steady you, one bite at a time.

wordCard.voice: The shipwreck. Fourteen days of storm, bread broken on a storm-battered deck, and two hundred and seventy-six people safe on Malta.

orig.note: Greek: be of good spirit, take heart. Paul says it twice on the ship (Acts 27:22, 25).
